title: Redd Foxx's club and the fusion quartet
summary: The group played Redd Foxx's club, later Cosby's partnership; audiences, before Corea and Hancock, were not ready.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah, the year '69, exactly, it was in '69. And I remember I had a gig at Redd Foxx's. Redd Foxx owned a club on La Cienega Blvd, in Los Angeles, called the Redd Foxx Club. And he was having, he did things with jazz things, and also he brought in comedians and everything like that. It was a nice room. But Bill Cosby came in partnership with Redd, and when Bill Cosby came in...I had worked there with Redd, and when Redd's business kind of went down...But Bill said he wanted me to stay there with the group. But he hooked up a partnership with Redd so he could keep the jazz, he wanted the jazz scene to keep happening because that was kind of like a hangout for Bill, too.
And Bill just loves being in that, and he treats it

right. Brought in all the big names and that, but I stayed in. The point I'm trying to make is, when I performed, I knew the people were trying to adjust their ears and also a visual thing. Because I know that they were sitting and looking at me strange.

No, it just wasn't conventional. It wasn't the sound...It wasn't like coming and listening to a piano, bass and drums, or whether it was a trio or what it was, or whatever it was. But we had some good arrangements, I thought.
People weren't as used to an electronic sound then?
Right, especially in a...I was using two keyboards. I wasn't pairing off of nobody, I didn't know anybody using two keyboards like that.
But there wasn't enough work to make it last?

It wasn't so cuh of that, I guess. I hadn't, I didn't have enough going for me, a record or a name or...I was experimenting, that's all I was doing. I was going through a phase that I had to get that on. And I...

A guy by the name of Lenny Hartley was playing the RMI, and Arthur Zikins(?) was playing the clavinet. And the drummer was Candy Finch. So musically, we knew where we were going. We had accepted it, and we were seriously...with the arrangements, and had us some good charts. And we knew we were kind of turning the people around because we were stretching with the music. We were playing fusion...
But the people weren't stretching with you...
Yeah, they weren't stretching. They hadn't been exposed to Chick Corea and Herbie Hancock.
